title: Longview Donors Turned $6 Million Into Room for Women and Children
thumbnailMessage: Longview built more room for women and children
summary: Hiway 80 Rescue Mission says supporters raised about $6 million and construction began on a 22,000-square-foot women-and-family residence hall designed to roughly double shelter capacity.
content:
A bare construction site in Longview represents an unusually concrete form of community help: local supporters moved a long-discussed shelter expansion from plans and fundraising into a building project for women and children who need a safe place to stay.

Hiway 80 Rescue Mission began clearing land in June for a new women-and-family residence hall at 119 Avenue D. KLTV reported that the mission had raised roughly $6 million for the first phase and expected the new facility to accommodate about 150 to 160 people, roughly double the current shelter’s approximately 80-bed capacity.

The public project record supports the scale of the work. The Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation lists a privately funded, 22,000-square-foot women’s dormitory at the site with an estimated construction cost of $7 million. The state registration identifies Hiway 80 Rescue Mission as the owner, Johnson & Pace as the design firm, a planned start date of June 15, 2026, and a planned completion date of May 31, 2027. The accessibility review is listed as complete.

Those figures describe a project, not a finished building. Cost, schedule and final capacity can change during construction, and the mission has not claimed that every remaining dollar is secured. What has already happened is still substantial: donors, staff, board members, volunteers, architects and contractors assembled enough support to begin a privately financed facility aimed at one of East Texas’ most persistent needs.

The expansion is designed around more than raw bed count. Executive director Brian Livingston told KLTV that the existing women’s shelter is regularly at or above capacity. The new two-story residence hall is planned with space for mothers and children upstairs and single women downstairs, with more private, hotel-style rooms instead of relying as heavily on large shared sleeping areas.

That design choice matters. A person entering emergency shelter may be carrying the effects of domestic violence, job loss, illness, eviction, addiction, family separation or another crisis. Privacy, safe storage, accessible bathrooms and the ability to keep children near a parent can affect whether a family remains long enough to stabilize. A dignified room is not a reward for perfect behavior; it is infrastructure for recovery.

Hiway 80 Rescue Mission has served East Texas since 1955. Its official history says the ministry began by providing food, shelter and Christian outreach to homeless men in Longview and now operates four campuses in Longview and Tyler. Its services include emergency shelter, meals, clothing, case management, recovery and discipleship programs, showers, laundry and help locating income and housing.

The organization’s faith identity is explicit and should not be obscured. It describes its programs as Christ-centered and its mission as offering a safe, supportive environment where homeless and hurting people can experience life transformation through Christ. People considering a referral or donation should be able to understand that model, along with any eligibility rules and which services are available regardless of participation in religious programming.

Case management is a central part of the mission’s stated approach. Staff work with residents to identify barriers, budget income and locate appropriate housing. That work is less visible than a new building but determines whether shelter becomes a temporary pause or a path toward stability. More beds without adequate case managers, security, child-friendly services and housing connections would leave the expansion incomplete.

The new residence hall is one phase of a broader vision. The mission has also discussed a commons building with an industrial kitchen and a dining hall able to seat 500 people, as well as a separate Tyler expansion. KLTV reported in June that fundraising was continuing for those later elements. Supporters should distinguish dollars already committed to the Longview residence hall from money still needed for future phases.

The hero in this story is collective. It is tempting to attach a large gift to one donor or a ceremonial photograph, but the verified record does not provide a complete public list of who gave what. RepWatchr will not invent one. The accomplishment belongs to the documented network of supporters and workers that raised about $6 million and put the first phase into construction.

Donors deserve clear receipts as the work continues. The mission should publish a project budget separating design, site work, construction, furnishings, contingency and fundraising costs. It should report how much is pledged, how much has been received and whether gifts are restricted to a particular phase. When construction ends, a final cost and certificate of occupancy will be more useful than a ceremonial estimate.

The state accessibility record creates another accountability marker. Texas’ architectural-barriers program requires plan review and inspection for covered projects. The mission should make accessibility part of the opening report: accessible entrances and rooms, bathroom design, routes for wheelchairs and strollers, visual and audible alarms, and any accommodations for residents with sensory or mobility disabilities. Safety should be measured before the first family moves in.

Operating costs need the same candor as capital costs. A building can be funded once, but beds require staffing, utilities, food, maintenance, insurance, transportation and programming every day. The mission should estimate the annual cost of operating the expanded facility and identify the mix of donations, grants, in-kind support and other revenue expected to sustain it. The most responsible capital campaign includes a plan to keep the doors open.

East Texans deciding whether to help should use the mission’s official channels. The organization lists its Longview administrative office at 3123 W. Marshall Avenue and a main phone number of 903-759-8101. Its official contact page lists 903-234-2583 for the women-and-family shelter. Anyone facing an immediate emergency should call 911; shelter availability and intake requirements should be confirmed directly with the mission.

Community help can also take forms other than money. Organizations can coordinate approved donations rather than dropping off unsorted items. Skilled volunteers can respond to posted needs. Employers and landlords can partner on jobs and housing. Churches and civic groups can support transportation, school supplies and family transition needs. Volunteers should follow the mission’s screening and privacy rules, especially around children and people fleeing violence.

The project should not be used to pretend that one nonprofit can solve homelessness by itself. Longview and surrounding counties still need affordable housing, behavioral-health care, addiction treatment, domestic-violence services, child care, transportation and jobs that cover rent. Public officials remain responsible for examining those systems. A privately funded shelter expansion is a strong community response, not permission for government or other institutions to look away.

Nor should residents be reduced to before-and-after marketing. The mission can report outcomes without exposing identities: average length of stay, exits to stable housing, returns to homelessness, employment connections, children served and unmet demand. Stories should be shared only with informed consent. Dignity includes control over one’s own name and history.

The planned completion date in the state record is May 31, 2027, while the mission previously described a six-to-18-month construction window. Until the building opens, the responsible way to follow progress is through milestones: foundation, framing, weatherproofing, utility work, accessibility inspection, furnishings, occupancy approval and a documented opening date.

What makes this an East Texas hero story is not a perfect institution or a promise that every problem is solved. It is neighbors investing enough time, money and work to create roughly twice as much room for women and children who may otherwise have nowhere safe to sleep. They converted compassion into plans, plans into permits and site work, and site work into a building now underway.

When the doors open, the public should receive the final ledger: actual cost, beds available, accessibility approval, operating plan and the outcomes the mission will measure. For now, the verified achievement is worth honoring. Longview supporters raised about $6 million, and a 22,000-square-foot residence hall is moving from aspiration toward shelter.
